title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned Developer Library, 1998. Keep it, take my pick or the familiar standard, or re-roll.

options.label: Developer Library, 1998
options.lineage: Late-90s vendor developer libraries (the MSDN Library era): topic browsers with a contents tree
options.thesis: Every article is a topic in a 1998 developer library: contents tree, a non-scrolling topic band, and a reading pane set like reference documentation.
materials: Verdana and Georgia, the 1996 core web fonts
beveled table borders and shaded rules
options.viewport: Black masthead; beneath it the sky-blue non-scrolling band with breadcrumb, title and a segmented section map; the contents tree in a left pane; the article opening in a white Georgia reading pane.
options.risk: Can read as early-2000s corporate docs rather than 90s web if the bevels and pixel icons are timid; Windows-flavoured for Linux readers.

raised.raise: One active band: a single moving 'you are here' state drives the tree selection, the band's section label and the section map together.
The route home: the band never scrolls away, and from any depth one tap in it reaches the contents.
Mark the one line that matters: highlighted code lines become a navy selection bar, the only strong fill inside code.
The flag where you stopped: your last position in each article is kept on this device and flagged in the tree and the section map when you return.
Extent-proportional map: each section's segment in the band is sized to that section's length, so the reader sees what is left before scrolling.
Reflow by whole panes: three panes step to two, then one, at fixed widths; a pane is never squeezed below its working width.

options.label: LinuxDoc HOWTO
options.lineage: Linux Documentation Project HOWTOs rendered by SGML-tools, 1996-99
options.thesis: The site as a Linux HOWTO: browser-default grey page, Times, numbered sections, and arrow button bars at the top and bottom.
materials: Times New Roman at browser default size
options.viewport: Grey page, a bar of pixel arrow buttons, the title as a plain h1, the numbered contents as a list, then section 1 in Times.
options.risk: Topped my own list, and it is where most '90s site' runs land: browser defaults read as unstyled unless the craft is visible.

options.label: Boxed-Software Manual
options.lineage: boxed software reference manuals with tabbed dividers
options.thesis: The article as a tabbed manual section, with a stepped tab rail mapping the whole extent.
options.viewport: The manual open at a coloured tab, text on a clear leaf, the tab rail down the fore edge.
options.risk: A print object, not a website; acetate layering costs reading contrast.
options.case: Closest challenger, from the 90s developer world, but a printed manual rather than a 90s website.
options.kept: Extent-proportional map: each section's segment sized to its length.

options.label: Hand-drawn Zine
options.thesis: A friend's napkin sketch: marker headings, doodled arrows, highlighter on the key line.
options.viewport: Marker headline, doodled diagram, a code box with one highlighted line.
options.risk: Mascot-led, while the kangaroo is favicon-only, and not 90s web.
options.case: Systems readers love zines, but the 90s brief and the favicon-only mascot rule it out.
options.kept: Mark the one line that matters: highlighted code lines get the strongest fill.

options.label: Daylight Section
options.lineage: architectural sections tracing a sunbeam through rooms
options.thesis: The article as one long building section, a sunbeam band marking how far you have read.
options.viewport: A ruled section drawing down the page, the beam crossing the current section.
options.risk: Neither a 90s website nor this audience's world.
options.case: Fuses poorly: both the pinned era and the engineers' world sit outside architectural drawing.
options.kept: One active band: one moving 'you are here' state across all wayfinding.

options.label: Mesophotic Deep Dive
options.thesis: Reading as descent: a depth axis for progress, sections as dive stages.
options.viewport: A vertical depth gauge beside the column, the current section at the thermocline.
options.risk: The metaphor outruns the content, and nothing about it is 90s.
options.case: Fuses only on the phrase 'deep dive'; loses identification and the era.
options.kept: The route home: a one-tap way back to the contents from any depth.

options.label: Cutting Bench Rail
options.thesis: Sections strung along a perforated rail, a tape flag where you stopped.
options.viewport: A perforated rail across the page, the current section punched into a white frame.
options.risk: An editing tool's costume around reading; not 90s web.
options.case: Loses both axes: engineers do not identify with film editing, and the rail fights the column.
options.kept: The flag where you stopped: your place is remembered and flagged on return.

options.label: Gridded Type Specimen
options.thesis: The page as a construction grid, letterforms and layout snapped to visible cells.
options.viewport: A huge grid-built title over faint construction lines.
options.risk: A poster rather than a document, and not 90s web.
options.case: Loses both: a type poster serves neither the reading nor the era.
options.kept: Reflow by whole panes: three panes to two to one, never a squeezed pane.

canonCard.label: The familiar retro standard
canonCard.thesis: What retro sites usually ship: every page is a Windows 98-style window on a teal desktop.
canonCard.viewport: Teal desktop with a maximised window: title bar, menu row, the article in a white sunken pane, a blocky progress bar in the status bar.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from other retro sites by design; the window chrome costs width on phones and dresses reading up as an operating system.
